intro: Who makes the models, how tiers differ, and how to reason about cost, speed and quality. (Names and prices change fast. Figures here are as of September 2026.)

1.summary: Labs, open vs closed models, model tiers, and access via API or Bedrock.

lesson.title: Who makes the models
lesson.body:
A handful of **frontier labs** build the most capable models: **Anthropic** (Claude), **OpenAI** (GPT), and **Google** (Gemini), with others like Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek and xAI.

Two ways models are released:

- **Closed** (proprietary): you use it through the maker's API or app, but you can't download it. Claude, GPT and Gemini work this way.
- **Open weights**: the trained model itself is downloadable, so you can run it on your own servers. Meta's Llama and many Mistral and DeepSeek models work this way.

Open weights give you control and privacy. Closed models are usually the most capable and need zero infrastructure.
lesson.pm: "Build on a closed API or host open weights?" is a real strategy decision about capability, cost, data control and team skills.

lesson.title: Tiers: big, balanced, fast
lesson.body:
Labs ship model **families** in tiers. Claude's current family:

- **Opus**: very capable, for hard reasoning and coding. Pricier.
- **Sonnet**: the balanced middle, strong and cheaper.
- **Haiku**: fastest and cheapest, great for simple, high-volume tasks.

(Anthropic also has an even more capable, more expensive top tier called Fable.)

The rule of thumb: **use the smallest model that meets your quality bar**, and route easy tasks to small models.

The same Claude models are available in several places: Anthropic's own **API**, **AWS Bedrock** (Amazon's cloud AI service, which your team uses), and Google Cloud. Same brain, different front door and billing.
lesson.pm: Model choice is a product decision: quality vs speed vs cost per request. Make it explicitly, per feature, instead of defaulting to the biggest model everywhere.

The programmatic way apps send requests to a model and get responses back, billed per token.

quiz.q: You need to sort 10 million support tickets into 5 categories cheaply. Which Claude tier should you test first?
quiz.why: Simple, high-volume work suits the smallest, cheapest tier. Test quality before moving up.

2.summary: Token pricing math, benchmarks vs evals, effort settings and model deprecation.

lesson.title: Pricing math and benchmarks
lesson.body:
Models are priced per **million tokens (MTok)**, with **output costing more than input**. As of September 2026:

- Claude Opus 5: $5 in / $25 out per MTok
- Claude Sonnet 5: $2 in / $10 out
- Claude Haiku 4.5: $1 in / $5 out

Quick math: a request with 2,000 input tokens and 1,000 output tokens on Sonnet 5 costs 0.002 × $2 + 0.001 × $10 = **$0.014**. Multiply by requests per day to get your bill.

**Benchmarks** are standardized tests (for example, SWE-bench for coding). They're useful for rough comparisons, but they're not *your* task. Your own **evals**, tests built from your real use cases, matter more.
lesson.pm: Always sketch the unit economics: tokens per request × requests per user × users. AI features can be cheap per call and expensive at scale.

lesson.title: Effort, speed and versions
lesson.body:
Many models let you choose an **effort** or **thinking** level. Higher effort means better answers on hard problems, but slower and costlier. Claude Code lets you switch model and effort (try `/model`).

**Latency** (how long until the answer arrives) matters for UX. Chat needs fast first words; a background job can wait.

Models are **versioned** and eventually **deprecated** (retired). A newer model may behave differently even with the same prompt, so teams re-run their evals before switching.
lesson.pm: Plan for model upgrades like dependency upgrades: budget time to re-test, and keep an eval set ready so switching is a measured decision, not a leap of faith.

cards.back: Million tokens: the unit AI models are priced in.
Input = what you send (prompt, context). Output = what the model writes. Output costs more per token.
A standardized test to compare models. Useful, but not the same as your real task.

A setting controlling how much a model thinks before answering: higher = better on hard tasks, slower and costlier.
When a model version is scheduled for retirement, so products need to migrate and re-test.
The delay before a response arrives. Critical for chat UX, less so for background jobs.

quiz.q: 1,000 input + 1,000 output tokens on a model priced $2 in / $10 out per million tokens. Cost?
What's the key difference between a benchmark and an eval?
options: An eval tests your own use cases
An eval is the official public score
They're two names for one thing
quiz.why: Benchmarks are public standard tests. Evals are built from your real tasks.

quiz.q: Which usually costs more per token?
quiz.why: Output is typically about 5× the input price. Cached input is cheapest.

quiz.q: A model is "deprecated". What does that mean?
options: It's been made cheaper to use
It's been retrained on new data
quiz.why: Deprecated models are on their way out, so plan and test a migration.

options: How long until a response arrives
How many tokens a reply contains
How often the model makes mistakes
